01 The threshold of sight

Small is a matter
of perspective.

Your eye can distinguish two points about 100 µm apart at a viewing distance of roughly 25 cm. Below that, details merge. A microscope takes you past that boundary.

Select an instrument

These are approximate resolving limits, not magnifications. Performance depends on the instrument and specimen. A smaller distance means finer detail can be distinguished.

1 mm = 1,000 µm1 µm = 1,000 nmµm = micrometre · nm = nanometre

Source: pp. 56, 63–65

02 A history of looking closer

Each new lens.
A new world.

Early magnifying glasses set the stage. Then a sequence of discoveries changed what humans could ask—and what they could see.

Scroll through the discoveries. The view changes with the story.

c. 1590
Early compound instruments

A lens meets another lens.

Traditionally linked to Dutch spectacle makers, early compound microscopes combine lenses in a tube. Their origins are debated, but the idea opens a powerful new direction.

↗ A new way to enlarge the small

1665
Robert Hooke · Micrographia

The tiny rooms get a name.

Looking at thin cork, Hooke sees a network of empty compartments. He calls them cells. His published drawings give readers a new view of familiar matter.

↗ The word “cell” enters science

1670s
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek

The hidden world is alive.

With carefully made single lenses, Leeuwenhoek observes tiny living organisms. His “animalcules” include organisms we now recognise as protozoa and bacteria.

↗ Microorganisms enter human view

1870s
Ernst Abbe

There is a limit to detail.

Abbe connects resolution to light’s wavelength and the lens’s aperture. Making an image larger cannot recover detail that the optics never resolved.

↗ Seeing more requires more than magnification

1930s
Ernst Ruska & Max Knoll

A different kind of beam.

The 1931 electron-microscope prototype uses electrons and magnetic lenses. Their much shorter wavelengths offer a route to details beyond conventional light microscopy.

↗ A new path to the ultrastructure of cells

1953
Frits Zernike · Nobel Prize in Physics

Transparent life becomes clearer.

Zernike receives the Nobel Prize for phase-contrast microscopy. Differences in how light passes through a living cell become visible contrast, without requiring stains.

↗ Observe living cells with greater contrast

Source: pp. 56–58 · Historical clarifications in source notes

03 Inside a compound microscope

Follow
the light.

The specimen stays tiny. An optical system forms a larger image. Select a component to discover what it contributes.

Start with illumination.

A lamp supplies light. In some microscopes, a mirror redirects an external light source. The light travels through the specimen toward the lenses above.

Two lenses, two jobs.

The objective forms a real, enlarged, inverted intermediate image. The eyepiece acts as a magnifier for this image, producing the final virtual view.

↳ The final image remains inverted relative to the specimen.
Simple microscopeOne magnifying lens, like a magnifying glass.
Compound microscopeObjective and eyepiece lens systems work together.

Source: pp. 58–60 · Image orientation clarified in source notes

05 Choose your question. Choose your instrument.

Three ways
to see deeper.

Do you need to see living cells, their internal structures, or a textured surface? The best microscope depends on the question.

Watch the living world.

Visible light passes through the specimen and glass lenses form the image. Observe cells, tissues, and moving organisms in a temporary mount.

Illumination
Visible light
Lens system
Glass lenses
Approximate resolution
0.2 µm
Living specimens?
Yes, with suitable preparation
Best suited to
Cells, tissues, pond organisms
Preparation
A thin specimen or temporary mount

Often the first choice in a school laboratory. Stains can improve contrast; phase contrast can reveal transparent living cells without staining.

Light has more than one trick.

Three optical techniques reveal different aspects of a specimen. These drawings illustrate contrast, not relative magnification.

Bright field

Light travels through the sample. Transparent unstained structures may show little contrast.

Ordinary optical view · conceptual

Phase contrast

Converts phase differences into brightness differences. Useful for transparent, living, unstained cells.

Greater contrast · conceptual

Fluorescence

Excitation light makes fluorescent labels emit light, highlighting selected structures against a dark background.

Selected structures glow · conceptual

Source: pp. 58–59, 63–66 · Approximate performance varies with instrument and sample

06 From specimen to slide

A moment of life.
Or a lasting record.

Preparation changes what you can observe. A temporary mount can show living processes; a permanent mount preserves structure for future study.

Observe it while it is fresh.

A thin specimen sits in a drop of water beneath a coverslip. Suitable living specimens can be observed for a short time, before the mount dries or changes.

Best for living processes · short-term observation

Lower the coverslip gently at an angle to reduce trapped air bubbles. Start with the lowest-power objective and bring the specimen into focus.

  1. Place a thin specimen in a drop of water.
  2. Lower the coverslip gently at an angle.
  3. Start at low power; adjust light and focus.
  4. Observe promptly and record what you see.

Carry it with care.

Hold the arm with one hand and support the base with the other.

Focus thoughtfully.

Use coarse focus at low power. At high power, use fine focus and keep the lens clear of the slide.

Keep the image clean.

Use lens paper for optics. Avoid touching lenses and protect the microscope when storing it.

Fieldwork idea · Compare leaf peelsObserve suitable monocot and dicot leaf epidermis. Compare cell shapes, their arrangement, guard cells, and stomatal distribution. Record what you actually see; features vary with the plant and the leaf surface.

Source: pp. 59–62, 68–69 · Preparation is an overview for supervised laboratory learning

07 The next frontier

Every answer
opens a new
question.

The story keeps growing. Better ways of seeing create better ways of understanding.

Bring the whole class to the eyepiece.

Digital microscopes put a live image on a screen, making observations easier to share, record, and discuss.

Go beyond conventional limits.

Super-resolution techniques reveal details below the usual diffraction limit of conventional light microscopy, using specialised illumination, labels, or reconstruction.

Small observations. Real-world impact.

✚Healthcare

Examine blood, sputum, and tissues; identify clues such as malaria parasites.

⌘Research

Study cells, plant tissues, stomata, and the structures that support living systems.

▦Manufacturing

Inspect electronic chips, metals, and plastics for quality and surface defects.

⌕Forensics

Compare small traces such as fibres, hair, and glass fragments.

≈Environment

Observe organisms and particles in water. A microscope view alone cannot prove water is safe to drink.

Source: pp. 66–67 · Digital microscopy, super-resolution, and applications

    Clarifications applied in this adaptation

    • Historical dates: the Abbe milestone uses “1870s”; Leica dates his published diffraction theory to 1873. Electron microscopy is placed in the 1930s, with the Ruska–Knoll prototype in 1931, rather than describing 1938 as the first invention. The 1953 milestone refers to Zernike’s Nobel Prize, not the year he invented phase contrast. The origins of the first compound microscope are described cautiously.
    • Image orientation: the final virtual image in a conventional compound microscope remains inverted relative to the original specimen. The eyepiece does not reverse the intermediate image a second time.
    • SEM: a focused electron beam scans the sample; detected secondary and backscattered electrons contribute to the image. SEM does not simply form a picture by mirror-like reflection, and standard SEM images are described as “3D-like.”
    • Limits and preparation: resolving distances are approximate and depend on the system and specimen. Conventional TEM/SEM preparation is unsuitable for watching living cells. Permanent mounting preserves structure, not ongoing life processes.
    • Models: illustrations are original explanatory diagrams, not measured micrographs. The field-of-view calculator is an idealised inverse-proportionality model. The resolution demonstration is qualitative. Optical zoom, focus, illumination, and resolving power should not be confused.
